title: Why Black musicians lacked conservatory training
summary: Goodwin says most Black families could not afford conservatory study, so the reading tests fell mostly on Black bands.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: And you said that more often happened you think to black bands than to white bands?
Right, right because the black man, let's face it, he didn't have money to spend to --
Well at least people didn't think he had.

Well, he didn't have money to spend, his parents didn't have money to spend. I'm talking about the masses of the blacks. There were some fortunate like black Duke, who could get music education, but the average family couldn't afford to send his kid to a conservatory to study
music, 'to study music for what, to come out and play in a jazz band', no, but you take now there's more people going to conservatories.
As I remember, I think it was four or five of Duke Ellington's men that were conservatory men.
Well, what you're saying is today a black musician or a black band would not be tested this way like back in the old, old days?
I see. Well that's a good thing right there. Baby, were you ready to say something?
